proposals.name: Recognizable Referents
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline names a person, place, organization, or topic a general reader can identify without prior context; low when the referent is obscure or unexplained; N/A when none is named.
proposals.rationale: Familiar referents can generate clicks independently of elite status or celebrity.

proposals.name: Immediate Personal Stakes
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline indicates implications for readers’ safety, health, money, rights, or daily life; low when consequences are distant; N/A when no personal implication is stated.
proposals.rationale: Perceived personal consequence is a readership motive missing from broad scale or domestic relevance.

proposals.name: Practical Actionability
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline promises advice, instructions, eligibility information, a warning, or a decision aid; low when it is purely descriptive; N/A when no practical implication appears.
proposals.rationale: Readers may click to decide what to do, regardless of conventional news value.

proposals.name: Explicit Information Gap
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline poses or implies a question, explanation, definition, or answer; low when it presents a complete proposition; N/A without an explanatory promise.
proposals.rationale: Answer-seeking is distinct from novelty and can directly motivate a click.

proposals.name: Outcome Open Loop
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline withholds a salient result while implying a narrative; low when the result is fully disclosed; N/A when no event or withheld result exists.
proposals.rationale: Curiosity from withheld resolution may attract readers despite low editorial salience.

proposals.name: Interpretive Clarity
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when readers can identify the asserted situation immediately; low when meaning depends on ambiguous pronouns, metaphor, or missing context; N/A without a substantive claim.
proposals.rationale: Clear headlines reduce comprehension costs and increase likelihood of opening.

proposals.name: Linguistic Accessibility
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high with common vocabulary and straightforward syntax; low with jargon, dense clauses, or unfamiliar terminology; N/A when the wording provides too little language to judge.
proposals.rationale: Casual-reader fluency affects clicks beyond topic importance.

proposals.name: Sensory Vividness
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when wording evokes concrete sights, sounds, or physical scenes; low when phrasing is abstract or administrative; N/A without a scene or physical condition.
proposals.rationale: Easily imagined scenes create attention without requiring novelty, violence, or human-interest coding.

proposals.name: Causal Coherence
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline states a clear cause, effect, or mechanism; low when it merely juxtaposes facts; N/A when no causal relation is presented.
proposals.rationale: A comprehensible causal promise helps readers see why opening the story matters.

proposals.name: Resolution Status
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline states a definite outcome or resolution; low when it reports only an allegation, warning, intention, or ongoing process; N/A without an event outcome.
proposals.rationale: Readers may prioritize completed consequential developments over generic ongoing coverage.

proposals.name: Dispute Intensity
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline explicitly presents disagreement, accusation, rejection, or clash; low when it depicts agreement or no contention; N/A without an evaluative conflict.
proposals.rationale: Conflict can motivate readership beyond violence, crisis, or legal proceedings.

proposals.name: Identity and Values
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline invokes group membership, beliefs, fairness, or moral self-conception; low when it contains no such cue; N/A without social or evaluative context.
proposals.rationale: Identity-relevant stories can motivate readership without elite actors, crisis, or domestic relevance.

proposals.name: Everyday Relatability
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the situation reflects an experience ordinary readers readily recognize; low when it is highly specialized or remote; N/A without a human experience.
proposals.rationale: Relatability can draw clicks separately from generic human-interest classification.

proposals.name: Evidence Cue
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline attributes a claim to a study, data, testimony, court, or named authority; low when it offers an unsupported assertion; N/A when no factual claim appears.
proposals.rationale: Credibility signals help readers judge whether a headline deserves attention.

proposals.name: Content Format Promise
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline signals maps, charts, video, a guide, quiz, or timeline; low when it offers no format cue; N/A without a presentation signal.
proposals.rationale: A promised format can increase clicks by clarifying immediate user value.

proposals.name: Very short event headline
proposals.instruction: Contains at most six whitespace-delimited words and a finite action verb, without a question or explanatory clause.
proposals.upstream_parent: Position/order in the day's homepage run

proposals.name: Explainer-question template
proposals.instruction: Begins with an explicit explanation frame such as “What is,” “How,” or “Why,” rather than a direct event report.

proposals.name: Feature-template wording
proposals.instruction: Uses a feature frame such as “The person who…” or “A life without…” instead of a conventional news lead.

proposals.name: First-person testimony
proposals.instruction: Contains “I,” “me,” “my,” “we,” or “our” within a quoted or testimonial frame.

proposals.name: BBC-attribution wording
proposals.instruction: Explicitly names BBC reporting or attribution, using phrases such as “tells BBC,” “BBC analysis,” or “BBC understands.”

proposals.name: Elite-name anchoring
proposals.instruction: Names a recognizable politician, royal, celebrity, or other prominent public figure.

proposals.name: Numeric-token formatting
proposals.instruction: Contains a numeral, currency symbol, percentage, measurement, or numeric time span.
proposals.upstream_parent: Data, SEO, or desk-specific packaging convention

proposals.name: Geographic desk syntax
proposals.instruction: Opens with a place name, nationality, or country-specific institution rather than an event or person.

proposals.name: Calendar-cycle wording
proposals.instruction: Names a holiday, annual observance, season, or fixed calendar occasion.

proposals.name: Running-story stage cue
proposals.instruction: Contains a continuation or closure marker such as “again,” “final,” “return,” “latest,” “second,” or “new rules.”
proposals.upstream_parent: Position within a multi-day running story

proposals.name: Curiosity Gap
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the headline creates a specific unanswered question while withholding its answer; low when it fully resolves the proposition. Does not apply when no answerable question is implied.
proposals.rationale: Unresolved information can motivate readers to click for closure.

proposals.name: Explanatory Promise
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the headline explicitly promises a how-or-why explanation or mechanism; low when it merely reports an event or status. Does not apply when no explanatory framing appears.
proposals.rationale: Explanatory value attracts readers seeking understanding, not merely updates.

proposals.name: Personal Consequence
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when consequences for readers’ safety, health, rights, or daily lives are explicit; low when effects remain remote or abstract. Does not apply when no reader-facing consequence is stated.
proposals.rationale: Perceived personal stakes predict attention beyond general domestic relevance.

proposals.name: Actionability
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the headline signals concrete guidance, eligibility, or a decision readers can use; low when it is purely descriptive. Does not apply absent advice, service, or decision framing.
proposals.rationale: Practical usefulness gives readers a direct reason to open the article.

proposals.name: Emotional Arousal
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when wording explicitly evokes fear, anger, disgust, joy, wonder, or amusement; low when wording is emotionally neutral. Does not apply when no affective cue is present.
proposals.rationale: Strong emotional activation can increase attention and readership independently of crisis or violence.

proposals.name: Moral Judgment
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the headline clearly signals injustice, wrongdoing, hypocrisy, or condemnation; low when it neutrally describes facts. Does not apply when no norm violation or evaluation appears.
proposals.rationale: Moral outrage and perceived fairness create broad, reader-relevant attention.

proposals.name: Controversy or Polarization
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when identifiable people or groups explicitly disagree, criticize, deny, protest, or clash; low when consensus or cooperation is presented. Does not apply absent disagreement.
proposals.rationale: Disagreement generates attention and participation beyond formal legal or institutional action.

proposals.name: Identity Resonance
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the headline names an identity group or lived-status category inviting group-based identification; low when no identity is salient. Does not apply when no identity category is explicit.
proposals.rationale: Group identification can make distant stories personally meaningful to readers.

proposals.name: Quoted Human Voice
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when first-person testimony or a vivid direct quote conveys an individual’s voice; low when the headline is paraphrased or impersonal. Does not apply without quotation or first-person voice.
proposals.rationale: Authentic voice increases intimacy, immediacy, and curiosity.

proposals.name: Accountability Attribution
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when responsibility, admission, denial, or blame is assigned to a specific actor; low when events lack an accountable agent. Does not apply when no responsibility claim appears.
proposals.rationale: Clear responsibility creates stakes and motivates readers to inspect evidence or consequences.

proposals.name: Narrative Momentum
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when wording indicates an unfolding sequence, escalation, pursuit, or imminent development; low when it gives a static description. Does not apply to timeless or purely background headlines.
proposals.rationale: Ongoing movement encourages readers to follow what happens next.

proposals.name: Visualizability
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the headline depicts a concrete scene, object, or physical action readily imagined; low when it concerns abstract ideas or processes. Does not apply without a concrete referent.
proposals.rationale: Easily pictured events are more attention-grabbing and memorable.

proposals.name: Processing Fluency
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when syntax and referents are immediately clear in ordinary language; low when wording is compressed, technical, ambiguous, or jargon-heavy. Does not apply when no substantive proposition can be parsed.
proposals.rationale: Easier comprehension lowers the effort required to choose the article.

proposals.name: Evidence Cue
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the headline cites a study, data, named source, or direct evidence; low when it presents an unsupported assertion. Does not apply when no evidential claim is made.
proposals.rationale: Credibility cues can attract readers seeking trustworthy information.

proposals.name: Format or Service Promise
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the headline advertises maps, charts, video, live coverage, Q&A, or another useful presentation. Low when no additional format or service is promised. Does not apply without such a cue.
proposals.rationale: Explicit presentation value gives readers a concrete reason to click.

proposals.name: Headline length band
proposals.instruction: Score the headline by word count, using short, medium, and long bands.

proposals.name: Quotation-mark framing
proposals.instruction: Record whether the headline prominently uses quotation marks around a claim, phrase, or testimony.

proposals.name: Explainer-question format
proposals.instruction: Mark headlines framed as “what is,” “how,” “why,” or an explicit question.

proposals.name: First-person testimony
proposals.instruction: Mark headlines containing first-person testimony or a personal quoted account.

proposals.name: Named-actor density
proposals.instruction: Count prominent named people, organizations, or official titles in the headline.

proposals.name: Geographic-name density
proposals.instruction: Count explicitly named countries, cities, regions, or geographic sites.

proposals.name: List-or-count framing
proposals.instruction: Mark headlines foregrounding a number, count, ranking, or enumerated set.

proposals.name: Data-package affordance
proposals.instruction: Mark explicit references to maps, charts, visualisations, guides, or other packaged formats.

proposals.name: Running-story continuity cue
proposals.instruction: Mark wording that signals continuation, aftermath, recurrence, or a final stage of an ongoing story.

proposals.name: Calendar-season cue
proposals.instruction: Mark explicit references to seasons, holidays, anniversaries, or a named day’s timing.
proposals.upstream_parent: Seasonal news cycle or calendar planning

proposals.name: Curiosity gap
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when a consequential fact is withheld but a clear question is created; low when the outcome is fully disclosed. Does not apply when no meaningful information is withheld.
proposals.rationale: Withheld but legible information can motivate clicks independently of institutional newsworthiness.

proposals.name: Explanatory promise
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when wording promises causes, mechanisms, background, or an answer; low when it merely announces an event. Does not apply without an explanatory frame.
proposals.rationale: Readers may click to resolve an explicit knowledge need rather than follow a breaking event.

proposals.name: Processing fluency
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when syntax and vocabulary are immediately easy to parse; low when compressed, ambiguous, or jargon-heavy. Does not apply when readability is unproblematic.
proposals.rationale: Low cognitive effort increases the chance that a homepage headline is understood and selected.

proposals.name: Referential completeness
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when people, events, and pronouns are identifiable from the headline alone; low when prior context is required. Does not apply when no potentially unclear referent appears.
proposals.rationale: A click decision requires enough context to know what the article concerns.

proposals.name: Concrete visuality
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the headline evokes a specific observable scene, object, or action; low when it states only abstract conditions. Does not apply when neither concrete nor abstract content predominates.
proposals.rationale: Vivid mental simulation can attract attention without elite actors, crisis, or scale.

proposals.name: Incongruous pairing
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when normally unrelated domains or entities are joined; low when the combination is conventional. Does not apply to single-domain headlines.
proposals.rationale: Unexpected combinations create distinctive hooks that may outperform conventional hard-news signals.

proposals.name: Firsthand voice
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when a participant’s quoted or clearly personal perspective is central; low when the headline uses only institutional narration. Does not apply without a personal perspective.
proposals.rationale: Personal voice can create intimacy and credibility beyond generic human-interest coding.

proposals.name: Ordinary-reader identification
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when an ordinary life role or experience lets readers imagine themselves involved; low when no relatable role appears. Does not apply when the story has no personal situation.
proposals.rationale: Self-relevance can drive readership even without domestic relevance or explicit economic impact.

proposals.name: Practical utility
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the headline promises guidance, choices, rules, or usable information; low when it offers no reader action. Does not apply to purely observational stories.
proposals.rationale: Utility-driven clicks reflect readers seeking help, not only curiosity about news events.

proposals.name: Personal consequence
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when bodily, household, financial, or safety effects are explicit; low when consequences remain institutional or distant. Does not apply if no consequence is stated.
proposals.rationale: Immediate personal stakes may predict clicking more directly than broad crisis or economic-impact labels.

proposals.name: Sensational framing
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when loaded, dramatic, superlative, or provocative wording heightens urgency; low when wording is restrained. Does not apply when language is neutral.
proposals.rationale: Attention-optimized framing can raise clicks while adding little conventional news value.

proposals.name: Positive entertainment
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when the framing promises amusement, wonder, warmth, or enjoyable discovery; low when neutral or grim. Does not apply when affective tone is indeterminate.
proposals.rationale: Enjoyment-oriented stories can rank highly despite lacking crisis, conflict, or institutional action.

proposals.name: Opinion clash
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when identifiable positions, judgments, or factions visibly oppose one another; low when no disagreement is framed. Does not apply without competing views.
proposals.rationale: Debate potential can attract readers even when the underlying event has modest news-value criteria.

proposals.name: Forward suspense
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when an imminent next step is signaled but its outcome remains uncertain; low when events are settled or retrospective. Does not apply without a future-oriented trajectory.
proposals.rationale: Anticipation supports return and click behavior beyond simple recency.

proposals.name: Memorable phrasing
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: High when wording is quotable, punning, or socially repeatable; low when generic. Does not apply when no distinctive phrasing appears.
proposals.rationale: Memorable headlines may earn clicks through conversational and sharing appeal.

proposals.name: HEADLINE
proposals.instruction: Update or continuation wording | DESCRIPTION: Contains markers such as “again,” “remains,” “return,” “amid,” or “new,” suggesting an ongoing story rather than a standalone item.

proposals.name: HEADLINE
proposals.instruction: Explainer-question format | DESCRIPTION: Uses a question or “What is/How...” construction that signals an explainer or background slot.

proposals.name: HEADLINE
proposals.instruction: Data-and-visuals framing | DESCRIPTION: Explicitly promises maps, charts, figures, or other structured presentation.

proposals.name: HEADLINE
proposals.instruction: First-person testimony framing | DESCRIPTION: Presents a quoted personal account beginning with “I,” “my,” or a similarly intimate testimonial construction.

proposals.name: HEADLINE
proposals.instruction: Ellipsis in headline | DESCRIPTION: Contains an ellipsis, especially where it dramatizes a personal statement or narrative reveal.

proposals.name: HEADLINE
proposals.instruction: Quoted loaded wording | DESCRIPTION: Places a vivid, contested, or emotionally charged phrase in quotation marks.

proposals.name: HEADLINE
proposals.instruction: Exact-number specificity | DESCRIPTION: Includes a conspicuous exact number, year, count, price, or time interval.

proposals.name: HEADLINE
proposals.instruction: Official-title concentration | DESCRIPTION: Names an institutional office, court, police body, military role, or other formal authority.

proposals.name: HEADLINE
proposals.instruction: International-place density | DESCRIPTION: Contains a foreign country, city, nationality, or geographically specific overseas location.

proposals.name: HEADLINE
proposals.instruction: Dramatic human-action verb | DESCRIPTION: Uses a vivid action verb such as “flee,” “cremated,” “chained,” “surrenders,” or “cloak” instead of a neutral reporting verb.

proposals.name: Curiosity gap
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline withholds an answer while supplying a compelling clue; low when it states the full payoff. Does not apply when no meaningful information gap is present.
proposals.rationale: Unresolved information can motivate readers to click beyond the editorial news value.

proposals.name: Emotional arousal
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline clearly evokes strong fear, anger, grief, awe, joy, or disgust; low when emotionally neutral. Does not apply when no emotional response is reasonably inferable.
proposals.rationale: Strong affect can drive readership independently of topic importance.

proposals.name: Surprise or incongruity
proposals.instruction: Scores high when people, events, or outcomes are presented in an unexpected combination; low when the content seems routine. Does not apply when the headline gives insufficient information to judge expectedness.
proposals.rationale: Unexpectedness may attract clicks even without novelty, crisis, or elite actors.

proposals.name: Practical personal utility
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline promises advice or information useful for an ordinary reader’s immediate choices; low when it offers no usable guidance. Does not apply when practical usefulness cannot be inferred.
proposals.rationale: Readers may prioritize actionable information over conventionally newsworthy content.

proposals.name: Perceived personal consequence
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline implies a direct effect on readers’ safety, rights, identity, or daily lives; low when consequences are remote. Does not apply when audience consequences are unspecified.
proposals.rationale: Perceived self-relevance can predict clicking beyond geographic or national relevance.

proposals.name: Narrative tension
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline presents an unresolved contest, dilemma, pursuit, or impending turn; low when the situation is settled. Does not apply without a discernible sequence or opposing forces.
proposals.rationale: Suspense can increase readership independently of violence, crisis, or institutional action.

proposals.name: Headline comprehensibility
proposals.instruction: Scores high when a careful reader can immediately understand the central event or claim; low when jargon, compression, or ambiguity obstructs understanding. Does not apply when the headline is too incomplete to interpret.
proposals.rationale: Easily processed headlines reduce cognitive friction and may attract broader readership.

proposals.name: Concrete specificity
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline names identifiable people, places, objects, and actions; low when it relies mainly on vague abstractions. Does not apply when the headline intentionally provides no concrete referent.
proposals.rationale: Specificity can make a story easier to imagine and evaluate from the headline alone.

proposals.name: Moral transgression
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline clearly signals betrayal, abuse, injustice, taboo, or serious norm violation; low when no norm violation appears. Does not apply when conduct is not morally interpretable.
proposals.rationale: Moral outrage can generate attention without depending on formal legal proceedings.

proposals.name: Identity polarization
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline activates opposing political, cultural, national, or group identities; low when it lacks an identity-based stance. Does not apply when no relevant group or position is stated.
proposals.rationale: Identity-relevant disagreement can motivate readership beyond generic political importance.

proposals.name: Social currency
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline offers material readers could readily discuss, display knowledge of, or share socially; low when it has little conversational value. Does not apply without a discernible audience or discussion angle.
proposals.rationale: Discussion and sharing incentives may help explain readership that editorial criteria miss.

proposals.name: First-person testimony
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline foregrounds a person’s direct testimony, quotation, or lived account; low when it is purely impersonal. Does not apply when no personal voice is present.
proposals.rationale: Perceived authenticity can attract readers independently of human-interest subject matter.

proposals.name: Explanatory payoff
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline promises to explain a cause, process, puzzle, or broader meaning; low when it merely reports an event. Does not apply without an explicit or strongly implied explanatory promise.
proposals.rationale: Readers may click for understanding rather than immediate event information.

proposals.name: Visual imaginability
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline evokes a vivid, easily pictured scene or transformation; low when it remains abstract or procedural. Does not apply when no scene or sensory image is suggested.
proposals.rationale: Vivid mental imagery can make otherwise low-priority stories unusually attention-grabbing.

proposals.name: Reader participation cue
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline invites readers to test, compare, identify, judge, or imagine themselves in the situation; low when it assigns no reader role. Does not apply without an explicit participatory cue.
proposals.rationale: Invitations to participate can convert passive interest into clicks.

proposals.name: Curiosity-gap identity withholding
proposals.instruction: The headline uses a pronoun or generic role while withholding the central person’s identifying name. This can reflect click-oriented copy editing rather than readership merit.

proposals.name: Explainer question framing
proposals.instruction: The headline begins with “What,” “How,” or “Why” to frame an explainer or analysis. This may mark an assigned format or desk workflow.

proposals.name: Ellipsis styling
proposals.instruction: The headline contains an ellipsis or deliberately unfinished phrase. This may be a house-style or engagement-oriented formatting habit.

proposals.name: Running-story sequence language
proposals.instruction: The headline uses explicit lifecycle terms such as “after,” “amid,” “begins,” “final,” “remains,” or “again.” These can reveal a story’s position in a multi-day editorial run.

proposals.name: Calendar-event wording
proposals.instruction: The headline explicitly names a holiday, season, anniversary, or calendar threshold such as “eve of” or “winter.” This can fingerprint seasonal commissioning and timing.

proposals.name: First-person testimony framing
proposals.instruction: The headline foregrounds first-person wording such as “I,” “my,” or a quoted personal account. This may identify an interview, testimony, or feature workflow.

proposals.name: Visual-package cue
proposals.instruction: The headline explicitly mentions maps, charts, pictures, video, or another presentation package. Such wording can reflect graphics production and homepage packaging.

proposals.name: Internal BBC attribution
proposals.instruction: The headline says that someone “tells BBC,” or labels the item as BBC analysis, investigation, or reporting. This can reveal internal access or promotional treatment.

proposals.name: Acronym-heavy shorthand
proposals.instruction: The headline contains multiple unexplained institutional abbreviations or compressed titles. This may fingerprint a wire, politics, or specialist-desk template.

proposals.name: Numeral-led headline format
proposals.instruction: The headline prominently leads with an exact count, price, date, age, or other numeral. This may reflect data, business, science, or auction-desk formatting independent of readership merit.

proposals.name: Direct quotation in headline
proposals.instruction: Scores 1.0 if the headline contains an explicit quotation mark, scores 0.0 if entirely indirect speech or objective summary.
proposals.rationale: Quotes create immediate intrigue, promising a human voice or dramatic statement that drives clicks.

proposals.name: Colloquial internet slang
proposals.instruction: Scores 1.0 if headline uses informal slang or internet jargon (e.g., "glow up"). Scores 0.0 if standard journalistic English is used.
proposals.rationale: Unconventional or modern vocabulary appeals directly to younger digital audiences, increasing organic click-through rates.

proposals.name: Psychological or medical condition
proposals.instruction: Scores 1.0 if a specific cognitive, anatomical, or medical anomaly is the central focus. Scores 0.0 for general health or policy news.
proposals.rationale: Readers are deeply drawn to quirky, relatable, or bizarre mysteries of the human body and brain.

proposals.name: Visual spatial anomaly
proposals.instruction: Scores 1.0 if headline describes an unusual physical or spatial phenomenon (e.g., webs over a landscape). Scores 0.0 for standard weather or disaster events.
proposals.rationale: Highly unusual visual imagery provokes intense reader curiosity, often prompting users to click for photos.

proposals.name: Historical or archaeological rarity
proposals.instruction: Scores 1.0 if headline mentions an ancient or historical artifact being discovered. Scores 0.0 if it refers to modern politics or standard news.
proposals.rationale: Everyday readers are fascinated by tangible links to the deep past and treasure-hunting narratives.

proposals.name: Frivolous celebrity dispute
proposals.instruction: Scores 1.0 if headline focuses on a petty argument involving an entertainer. Scores 0.0 if the dispute involves serious geopolitical or institutional consequences.
proposals.rationale: Soft-news gossip provides highly clickable entertainment value and escapism that formal criteria might undervalue.

proposals.name: Viral internet challenge
proposals.instruction: Scores 1.0 if the headline references a social media trend, challenge, or slang. Scores 0.0 if it covers offline or traditional institutional events.
proposals.rationale: Readers actively track digital cultural phenomena, seeking context for the bizarre things they see online.

proposals.name: Explainer format
proposals.instruction: Scores 1.0 if the headline starts with "What is", "How", or poses a direct question. Scores 0.0 if it is a declarative statement of fact.
proposals.rationale: Questions explicitly promise to resolve reader ignorance regarding a trending topic, driving high curiosity clicks.

proposals.name: Trivial physical characteristic
proposals.instruction: Scores 1.0 if the headline focuses on a lighthearted trait (e.g., weight, height, size). Scores 0.0 if it concerns serious discrimination or institutional policy.
proposals.rationale: Bizarre or highly specific physical facts offer low-stakes, highly shareable entertainment that readers eagerly consume.

proposals.name: Idiosyncratic profession limitation
proposals.instruction: Scores 1.0 if headline highlights a professional performing their job despite a severe physical limitation. Scores 0.0 if it covers standard career achievements.
proposals.rationale: Overcoming extreme adversity to achieve a specific goal is a powerful human interest narrative that drives engagement.

proposals.name: Domestic US political chaos
proposals.instruction: Scores 1.0 if headline mentions US political figures alongside conflict, legal issues, or multiple battles. Scores 0.0 for routine international diplomacy.
proposals.rationale: Global audiences click heavily on the continuous, high-stakes drama surrounding US political figures.

proposals.name: Positive environmental anomaly
proposals.instruction: Scores 1.0 if a nation or group is praised for a surprising positive achievement (e.g., education superpower). Scores 0.0 for standard conflict news.
proposals.rationale: Counter-intuitive success stories provide uplifting escapism, driving clicks from readers fatigued by negative news.

proposals.name: Direct threat to human life
proposals.instruction: Scores 1.0 if the headline explicitly describes imminent danger to individuals (e.g., bushfire zone, army actions). Scores 0.0 for abstract political threats.
proposals.rationale: Imminent danger triggers a primal, morbid curiosity that compels readers to seek immediate details.

proposals.name: Financial windfall
proposals.instruction: Scores 1.0 if headline details an unexpected or massive monetary gain, auction, or discovery. Scores 0.0 if it concerns macroeconomic indicators or regulations.
proposals.rationale: Massive financial figures and rare wealth capture reader attention and aspirational curiosity far better than policy.

proposals.name: Prominent named individual
proposals.instruction: Scores 1.0 if a globally recognizable first name (e.g., Melania, Trump) leads the headline. Scores 0.0 if it relies on formal titles or lesser-known names.
proposals.rationale: Name recognition provides an immediate cognitive shortcut, making soft news or gossip highly clickable.

proposals.name: Listicle & Data Format Markers
proposals.instruction: Headline uses pluralized aggregates or explicitly references charts, maps, or visual summaries.
proposals.upstream_parent: Data-journalism or features desk production habits

proposals.name: Named-Individual Frame
proposals.instruction: Headline isolates a specific named person's experience rather than a broad institutional event.

proposals.name: Quoted Epithet or Slang
proposals.instruction: Headline contains a prominent scare-quote that acts as a tease rather than summarizing hard news.

proposals.name: "How" Explainer Prefix
proposals.instruction: Headline starts with or prominently features the word "How" indicating an analytical or historical piece.

proposals.name: Sequential Factual Terminators
proposals.instruction: Headline features events implying an ongoing running story has updated, using words like revised, new, or looming.

proposals.name: Hyperbolic Soft-News Adjectives
proposals.instruction: Uses informal, sensational modifiers (e.g., glow up, explosive) absent from standard hard news headlines.

proposals.name: Explicit Death & Violence Lexicon
proposals.instruction: Headline explicitly uses words like dead, raped, or suicide instead of neutral institutional terminology.

proposals.name: Esoteric Condition Neologisms
proposals.instruction: Headline introduces a highly specific, unfamiliar medical or scientific condition name by name.

proposals.name: Generic Protest Outcry Keywords
proposals.instruction: Headline relies on generic expressions of conflict (outcry, warning, fears) without specifying an action.

proposals.name: Observational Weather Anomaly
proposals.instruction: Headline emphasizes highly unusual visual or seasonal phenomena (floods, warmth) lacking direct human action.

proposals.name: Quoted first-person extreme human interest
proposals.instruction: Headlines containing a first-person quote (e.g., "I", "my") combined with visceral, emotional, or existential stakes score high. Score low if the quote is strictly a factual policy or event statement.
proposals.rationale: Extreme human vulnerability directly provokes reader curiosity and emotional clicks.

proposals.name: High-recognition celebrity and pop culture scandal
proposals.instruction: Headlines featuring globally recognized pop-culture figures (e.g., Heidi Klum, R. Kelly) involved in entertainment, lifestyle, or scandal score high. Score low for lesser-known niches or strictly political figures.
proposals.rationale: Readers habitually click on highly familiar names regardless of strict news value.

proposals.name: Data-driven visual format
proposals.instruction: Headlines explicitly promising charts, maps, or visual data summaries score high. Score low for text-only analyses or investigations. Does not apply to headlines lacking format promises.
proposals.rationale: Readers click heavily for accessible, visual summaries of complex ongoing events like elections.

proposals.name: Geographically remote elite violence
proposals.instruction: Institutional action or violence involving elite actors in Africa, remote regions, or secondary global conflicts scores low. Does not apply to domestic or top-tier geopolitical conflicts.
proposals.rationale: BBC readership strongly favors domestic or major geopolitical crises over remote regional politics.

proposals.name: Bizarre novelty and human oddities
proposals.instruction: Headlines describing extremely rare medical conditions, strange talents, or peculiar animal facts score high. Score low for standard human interest or routine science features.
proposals.rationale: Curiosity gaps about unprecedented, bizarre human and animal phenomena drive massive click-through rates.

proposals.name: Bureaucratic updates and minor scandals
proposals.instruction: Resignations, proposed deals, or legal proceedings of secondary officials without mass impact or top-tier celebrity score low. Does not apply to heads of state or major policy shifts.
proposals.rationale: Dry institutional mechanics or minor elite actions usually fail to attract mass readership.

proposals.name: Offline viral trends and social media hooks
proposals.instruction: Headlines referencing surprising, shocking, or viral social media trends (e.g., condom snorting, QAnon) score high. Score low for routine tech updates or institutional policy.
proposals.rationale: Readers click to understand bizarre online phenomena bleeding into mainstream offline discourse.

proposals.name: Direct threat proximity to the domestic reader
proposals.instruction: Headlines detailing immediate, mass-casualty threats (e.g., war, extreme weather, crashes) score high. Score low for distant, potential, or localized environmental threats.
proposals.rationale: Urgent, life-threatening events trigger a survival-driven impulse for immediate reader engagement.

proposals.name: Unusual juxtapositions in headlines
proposals.instruction: Headlines combining two highly incongruous concepts (e.g., a chef losing smell, a musician playing with toes) score high. Score low if the juxtaposition is a standard political pairing.
proposals.rationale: Cognitive dissonance creates a strong curiosity gap that compels readers to click.

proposals.name: Explicit numeric curiosities and superlatives
proposals.instruction: Headlines featuring specific numbers indicating unusual scale (e.g., 52-year first) or quirky size claims (e.g., flight attendant size) score high. Score low for routine tallies or standard dates.
proposals.rationale: Precise numbers and quirky superlatives signal a contained, highly unique story that drives clicks.

proposals.name: Horrific or gruesome crime details
proposals.instruction: Headlines featuring violent death, disaster, or abuse combined with graphic adjectives or visceral nouns score high. Score low for sanitized, institutional reports of violence.
proposals.rationale: Morbid curiosity about the explicit details of violence and death reliably drives high readership.

proposals.name: Novelty and wonder in nature and archaeology
proposals.instruction: Headlines highlighting spectacular discoveries (e.g., treasure hoards, unique animal traits) or shocking natural phenomena score high. Score low for routine ecological studies or gradual climate changes.
proposals.rationale: Positive or awe-inspiring discoveries offer strong escapist appeal, driving high reader engagement.

proposals.name: Royal and domestic political melodrama
proposals.instruction: Headlines featuring royal families or top-tier politicians in personalized, human-interest drama score high. Score low for routine policy or diplomatic news.
proposals.rationale: Readers heavily click domestic political gossip and personalized royal melodrama over dry institutional action.

proposals.name: Wealth and luxury juxtaposed with destruction
proposals.instruction: Headlines combining high-value luxury assets with disaster or decay score high. Score low for standard financial news or ordinary property damage.
proposals.rationale: The dramatic contrast of extreme wealth with ruin presents an irresistible narrative for readers.

proposals.name: Headline linguistic clickbait markers
proposals.instruction: Headlines using dramatic quotation marks, cliffhanger ellipses, or imperative mysteries score high. Score low for declarative, straightforward event reporting.
proposals.rationale: Stylistic curiosity gaps directly prompt the reader to click to resolve the unknown information.

proposals.name: First-person direct quote
proposals.instruction: Headline begins with or prominently features a first-person pronoun inside quotation marks.
proposals.upstream_parent: Editorial commissioning of personalized human-interest features

proposals.name: Quizzical or 'how' framing
proposals.instruction: Headline uses a question mark or begins with words like 'How', 'Why', or 'What'.
proposals.upstream_parent: Analytical or explanatory feature desks (often published off-cycle)

proposals.name: Unusual medical or psychological condition
proposals.instruction: Headline names a rare disease, obscure psychological condition, or specific sensory loss.
proposals.upstream_parent: Slow-burn science and health feature desks

proposals.name: Obscure foreign institutional actor
proposals.instruction: Headline focuses on a little-known non-Western politician or local foreign institution taking administrative action.
proposals.upstream_parent: Dedicated foreign desks reporting required institutional news

proposals.name: Geographic qualifier in headline
proposals.instruction: Headline explicitly names a country, city, or specific region before the main subject.
proposals.upstream_parent: International desk formatting habits to disambiguate stories

proposals.name: Explainer keyword and chart format
proposals.instruction: Headline explicitly uses words like 'maps', 'charts', or 'explainer' to promise visual data.
proposals.upstream_parent: Visual and data journalism team production formats

proposals.name: Social media and internet culture topic
proposals.instruction: Headline names a specific social network, app, or references a viral internet trend.

proposals.name: Celebrity novelty or entertainment format
proposals.instruction: Headline mentions a recognizable celebrity name alongside a trivial action, event, or aesthetic change.
proposals.upstream_parent: Entertainment and arts desks (soft news cycle)

proposals.name: Global North versus Global South violence
proposals.instruction: Headline focuses on political violence, coups, or conflict exclusively in the developing world.

proposals.name: Rare natural or ecological threat
proposals.instruction: Headline describes a highly specific animal death, botanical anomaly, or ecological event.

proposals.name: Hyperbolic or Idiomatic Phrasing
proposals.instruction: Headlines using dramatic, colloquial, or metaphorical vocabulary ("glow up", "chaos", "queen") score 1; neutral institutional language scores 0.
proposals.rationale: Sensational or informal wording drives casual reader clicks by triggering emotional curiosity.

proposals.name: Unresolved First-Person Hook
proposals.instruction: First-person quotes or ambiguous narratives ("If I lock...") score 1; straightforward reported facts score 0.
proposals.rationale: High curiosity gaps compel audiences to click to uncover the full narrative context.

proposals.name: Bizarre or Novel Subject
proposals.instruction: Headlines describing highly unusual personal traits or unique phenomena ("plays... with toes") score 1; routine events score 0.
proposals.rationale: Intrigue and human oddities reliably attract click-throughs from a broad audience.

proposals.name: Ubiquitous Tech Platforms
proposals.instruction: Mentions of widely used consumer tech ("WhatsApp", "online posts") score 1; niche or institutional entities score 0.
proposals.rationale: Broadly relevant subjects personally resonate with everyday readers, increasing clicks.

proposals.name: Cultural Events or Industry News
proposals.instruction: Headlines mentioning entertainment, celebrities, or sports score 1; political or hard news scores 0.
proposals.rationale: Soft news topics often generate high-volume, impulsive reader engagement outside editorial priorities.

proposals.name: US Domestic Reader Focus
proposals.instruction: Headlines explicitly naming US institutions, geography, or figures score 1; non-US or general international topics score 0.
proposals.rationale: BBC's online audience is heavily American; US-centric topics drive disproportionate readership.

proposals.name: Direct Question Format
proposals.instruction: Headlines formatted as an explicit question ("What is...?", "How did...?") score 1; declarative statements score 0.
proposals.rationale: Questions create an immediate information gap, psychologically prompting the reader to click.

proposals.name: Quirky Science or Psychology
proposals.instruction: Studies on pets, human biology, or cognitive phenomena score 1; policy or political analysis scores 0.
proposals.rationale: Readers frequently share and click relatable, lighthearted, or surprising scientific trivia.

proposals.name: Classic Listicles and Explainers
proposals.instruction: Headlines containing words like "maps", "charts", "puzzle", or "what is" score 1; breaking event summaries score 0.
proposals.rationale: Readers actively seek formatted, easily digestible visual explainers for complex events.

proposals.name: High-Name-Recognition Celebrity
proposals.instruction: Mentions of global pop-culture figures ("Heidi Klum", "Axl Rose") score 1; obscure politicians or local figures score 0.
proposals.rationale: Mainstream celebrity fame reliably generates clicks, even for trivial or soft news.

proposals.name: Relatable Daily Life Impact
proposals.instruction: Headlines about travel disruptions, prices, or weather score 1; foreign conflicts or policy debates score 0.
proposals.rationale: Readers prioritize news that immediately affects their personal routines and daily logistics.

proposals.name: Geographically Obscure Conflict
proposals.instruction: Headlines mentioning violence in unfamiliar regions (CAR, Gabon) score 1; Western or major powers score 0.
proposals.rationale: Editors may push obscure foreign crises, but readers often bypass them for familiar news.

proposals.name: Descriptive Label Format
proposals.instruction: Headlines starting with a subject name followed by a colon score 1; standard subject-verb sentences score 0.
proposals.rationale: Analytical or opinion column formats often fail to trigger the urgency needed for clicks.

proposals.name: Distant Historical Discoveries
proposals.instruction: Headlines about unearthed artifacts or historical figures score 1; contemporary political or social events score 0.
proposals.rationale: Archaeological and historical news is editorially valued but typically draws low casual readership.

proposals.name: Promoted Commentary or Analysis
proposals.instruction: Headlines focusing on subjective opinion, feelings, or personal memoir score 1; objective factual reporting scores 0.
proposals.rationale: Readers generally seek breaking facts over external analysis, resulting in lower click rates.

proposals.name: Colloquial pop-culture slang
proposals.instruction: Headline contains modern informal idioms, pop-culture terms, or internet slang (e.g., "glow up", "queen of").
proposals.upstream_parent: Editorial push for younger demographic appeal

proposals.name: High-velocity active disaster syntax
proposals.instruction: Uses present-progressive verbs and chaotic terms (e.g., "barrels towards", "travel chaos") indicating an ongoing, uncontrolled situation.
proposals.upstream_parent: Breaking news desk urgency and live updating format

proposals.name: Q-format or buzzword explainer
proposals.instruction: Headline is phrased as a question ("What is...") or focuses on a highly searched viral buzzword (e.g., Aphantasia, QAnon).
proposals.upstream_parent: Search engine optimization (SEO) and traffic acquisition strategy

proposals.name: Rule-of-three curiosity gap
proposals.instruction: Uses the exact phrase structure "The [noun] who [unexpected action]" to promise a human-interest payoff not present in the text itself.
proposals.upstream_parent: Magazine or features desk house-style templates

proposals.name: Domestic micro-betting hook
proposals.instruction: Explicitly mentions maps, charts, or interactive data formats for a major political event (e.g., US election results in maps).

proposals.name: Confrontational cross-domain row
proposals.instruction: Headline explicitly pairs celebrities/politicians from different domains with the word "row" or "clash" (e.g., Axl Rose and Steven Mnuchin).
proposals.upstream_parent: Viral social media aggregation desk monitoring

proposals.name: Personal domestic tragedy quote
proposals.instruction: Leads with a dramatic first-person quote detailing extreme survival or violence (e.g., "If I lock this door, he dies").
proposals.upstream_parent: High-prominence editorial curation of lead video or multimedia

proposals.name: Bureaucratic institutional probe wording
proposals.instruction: Uses passive, clinical language regarding formal meetings or institutional actors (e.g., "weapons watchdog hosts meeting").
proposals.upstream_parent: Slower-paced investigative or diplomatic desk cadence

proposals.name: Extreme domestic policy impact framing
proposals.instruction: Frames macro-level government policy or economic shifts as an immediate, personal household threat (e.g., "No heat to eat").
proposals.upstream_parent: High-prominence curation of domestic cost-of-living crisis

proposals.name: Unexplained foreign capital acronym
proposals.instruction: Headline leads with an abbreviated foreign nation or conflict zone (e.g., "CAR", "DRC") without spelling it out.
proposals.upstream_parent: Lower-prominence placement on the international desk

proposals.name: Voyeuristic or bizarre micro-human-interest framing
proposals.instruction: Headlines featuring bizarre, quirky, or highly unusual specific individuals (often using "who" clauses) score high; routine biographies or standard profiles score low; does not apply to general human-interest topics.
proposals.rationale: Clickbait and high readership are often driven by extreme novelty or bizarre voyeuristic scenarios.

proposals.name: Celebrity combined with incongruous civic conflict
proposals.instruction: Headlines placing recognizable celebrity names into unexpected clashes with political figures or legal consequences score high; routine entertainment news scores low.
proposals.rationale: Clashes between pop culture and elite politics generate high cross-domain reader curiosity and clicks.

proposals.name: Unfiltered first-person trauma or threat quote
proposals.instruction: Headlines consisting entirely or primarily of a shocking first-person quote score high; descriptive indirect speech scores low; does not apply to general opinions.
proposals.rationale: Raw emotional quotes create immediate narrative tension, bypassing cognitive filters to drive rapid clicking.

proposals.name: Travel or transit disruption affecting many
proposals.instruction: Headlines about systemic travel chaos, grounded flights, or mass cancellations score high; standard policy or automotive news scores low.
proposals.rationale: Travel disruptions possess immediate, practical utility, prompting massive rapid clicking from affected demographics.

proposals.name: Hyper-unusual anthropological or scientific discovery
proposals.instruction: Headlines describing incredibly rare archaeological, physiological, or bizarre natural phenomena score high; routine science updates score low.
proposals.rationale: Internet audiences heavily share and click on awe-inducing, highly visual anomalies or historical mysteries.

proposals.name: Major US political figures or legal clashes
proposals.instruction: Mentions of major US politicians (e.g., Trump) or their legal battles score high; non-US political figures in routine governance score low.
proposals.rationale: US political dramas command massive global audience attention and emotional engagement, driving clicks.

proposals.name: Domestic relatable daily-life novelty or slang
proposals.instruction: Headlines featuring relatable internet slang ("glow up") or intriguing everyday psychology score high; formal sociological analysis scores low.
proposals.rationale: Readers click heavily on easily digestible, relatable pop-culture or internet-trend phenomena.

proposals.name: Elite figure with quirky, non-violent personal hook
proposals.instruction: Headlines featuring top-tier elites in domestic, personal, or pop-culture scenarios score high; elites in routine policy news score low.
proposals.rationale: Gossip or humanizing quirks about recognizable elites trigger voyeuristic curiosity that outpaces hard news clicks.

proposals.name: Prurient, sexual, or bodily scandal elements
proposals.instruction: Headlines mentioning sexual abuse, breastfeeding, or bodily functions score high; standard legal or political proceedings score low.
proposals.rationale: Readers disproportionately click on headlines containing highly emotive or taboo prurient elements.

proposals.name: Reader-utility format promise (charts, maps, puzzles)
proposals.instruction: Headlines explicitly promising lists, charts, puzzles, or interactive formats score high; text-only standard reports score low.
proposals.rationale: Readers click heavily on visual, interactive, or easily digestible utility formats for major ongoing stories.

proposals.name: Internet-native cultural phenomenon or mystery
proposals.instruction: Headlines referencing viral trends, online mysteries (e.g., QAnon), or bizarre online behaviors score high; standard tech business news scores low.
proposals.rationale: Readers actively click to understand weird cultural phenomena dominating their social media feeds.

proposals.name: Explicit prominent dollar figure or numeric record
proposals.instruction: Headlines containing explicit, large monetary figures or time-based records score high; vague references to "huge" amounts score low.
proposals.rationale: Concrete numbers provide immediate stakes and quantified scale, lowering cognitive barriers to clicking.

proposals.name: Direct domestic or local geographic naming
proposals.instruction: Headlines explicitly naming "US", "UK", or domestic regions score high; foreign capital cities or distant regions score low.
proposals.rationale: Readers prioritize local relevance; domestic geographic triggers reliably outperform foreign news in clicks.

proposals.name: High-stakes action verb signaling immediate danger
proposals.instruction: Headlines using active threat verbs like "flees", "looms", or "barrels" score high; static passive verbs score low.
proposals.rationale: Evocative action verbs immediately signal urgent personal relevance, driving rapid defensive information-seeking.

proposals.name: Direct hook ending in unresolved cliffhanger
proposals.instruction: Headlines structured as a teasing cliffhanger score high; complete descriptive sentences score low; does not apply to standard titles.
proposals.rationale: Cliffhangers exploit the curiosity gap, compelling readers to click purely to resolve the informational tension.

proposals.name: LENGTH-DEPENDENT MYSTERY GAP
proposals.instruction: Headline relies on a short noun phrase or fragments without explaining the context, leaving the reader to click to resolve the mystery.
proposals.upstream_parent: EDITORIAL PACKAGING (headline space constraints or teasing strategy)

proposals.name: DEFINITE-ARTICLE BIOGRAPHICAL FRAMING
proposals.instruction: Headline begins with "The" and describes an individual's unique personal trait, hobby, or specific situation rather than a public role.
proposals.upstream_parent: DESK OR BEAT (Features, Lifestyle, or Human Interest desk)

proposals.name: NAMED-CELEBRITY CONFRONTATION
proposals.instruction: Headline features two recognizable named individuals (or a celebrity and an official) primarily engaged in a verbal spat, row, or social media dispute.
proposals.upstream_parent: DESK OR BEAT (Entertainment or pop culture desk)

proposals.name: ENCAPSULATED DIRECT QUOTATION
proposals.instruction: Headline uses quotation marks to enclose a dramatic, hyperbolic, or evocative phrase without attributing the speaker in the text.
proposals.upstream_parent: EDITORIAL PACKAGING (teasing strategy or click-bait framing)

proposals.name: OBLIQUE PRONOUN REFERENCES
proposals.instruction: Headline uses first or second-person pronouns ('I', 'he', 'my') or refers to a specific named person by first name only, omitting their institutional role.
proposals.upstream_parent: DESK OR BEAT (Features or soft news)

proposals.name: DOMESTIC POLITICO-CORPORATE DISPUTE
proposals.instruction: Headline focuses on a localized or domestic dispute, legal claim, or tariff involving airlines, tech platforms, or named US/UK politicians.
proposals.upstream_parent: DESK OR BEAT (Domestic business or political desk)

proposals.name: INSTITUTIONAL HEADLINE NOMINALIZATION
proposals.instruction: Headline leads with a formal institution or country as a subject paired with an abstract institutional action noun or a named official.
proposals.upstream_parent: DESK OR BEAT (Foreign desk or institutional hard news)

proposals.name: LIST-FORM PRONOUN RESOLUTION
proposals.instruction: Headline highlights a specific group or person being targeted by a policy or disaster but omits the geographic or political context required to identify them.
proposals.upstream_parent: EDITORIAL PACKAGING (space constraints omitting dull context)

proposals.name: INTERROGATIVE OR DEFINITIONAL FORMAT
proposals.instruction: Headline is phrased as a question or explicitly seeks to define a specific term, concept, or medical/psychological condition.
proposals.upstream_parent: DESK OR BEAT (Explainer or vertical news desk)

proposals.name: NUMERIC FRAMING OF ONGOING EVENT
proposals.instruction: Headline uses explicit numerals to denote a time frame, an amount of money, or a count of items tied to a currently unfolding event.
proposals.upstream_parent: POSITION OR ORDER (in a running news cycle)
